title: Disability Tax Credit
summary: Observe → Record → Certify → Apply → Follow Up
subtitle: Turn daily life into evidence a form can use

blocks.text: A diagnosis may be one line long. A Tuesday involving medication, supervision, recovery time and twelve careful steps is rarely so considerate.

The Disability Tax Credit, or DTC, is a tax credit that cannot be paid out as a refund on its own. It can lower the income tax of the approved person or, in some cases, a family member who supports them. It is for severe, long-lasting conditions. It is not a monthly disability payment, and a diagnosis alone does not get you approved.

DTC areas include walking, speaking, hearing, seeing, eating, dressing, using the washroom and the mental skills needed for daily life. Life-sustaining therapy and the combined effect of several limits each have their own routes.

items.title: “Only visible or physical disabilities can qualify.”
items.text: The DTC covers physical, sensory and mental functions. The test is how much the condition limits daily life, as certified under the law, not whether a stranger can see it.

blocks.text: Learn what the CRA looks for, and your application can describe your real days instead of just naming a diagnosis.
blocks.detail: Specific, truthful detail about how often, how long and with what help gives your practitioner something concrete to certify.
blocks.extra: Next, the five lenses that turn your days into evidence.

sections.title: Show the Pattern, Not Just the Label

blocks.text: A marked restriction usually means you cannot do an activity, or it takes about three times as long as it would for someone your age without the condition. That is true even with the right therapy, devices and medicine. It must be there all or almost all of the time, usually at least 90%, and last or be expected to last at least 12 months in a row.

items.title: FUNCTION
items.text: Name the everyday task that is affected and what happens in ordinary life.

items.title: FREQUENCY
items.text: Note how often the problem happens, on better days and on harder days.

items.title: TIME
items.text: Explain how much longer the task takes than it would for someone your age, where that test applies.

items.title: SUPPORT
items.text: List the therapy, medicine, devices, reminders, supervision or hands-on help you already use.

items.title: DURATION
items.text: Say when the pattern began and whether it has lasted, or will last, at least 12 months in a row.

blocks.text: Two or more serious limits can sometimes add up to the same thing as a marked restriction. Each limit must meet the CRA’s rules for combined effects, and small hassles do not add up to eligibility by committee.

items.title: “A medical diagnosis guarantees DTC approval.”
items.text: A health practitioner certifies the condition and its effects, but the CRA decides who qualifies under the legal rules. Clear, honest detail about daily life helps more than a diagnosis name travelling alone.

blocks.text: For life-sustaining therapy, the test looks at why you need it, how often and how much time it takes. People with type 1 diabetes are treated as meeting the therapy test for 2021 and later years.

sections.title: Give Each Person the Right Job

items.title: APPLICANT
items.text: Fills in Part A, names who may claim the amount and gives consent. You can start online and give your practitioner a reference number.

items.title: MEDICAL PRACTITIONER
items.text: Fills in Part B for the right area using their own judgment. They may charge a fee, so ask first.

items.title: CRA
items.text: Reviews the form and decides whether the rules and years are met. The CRA may ask for more information.

items.title: AFTER THE DECISION
items.text: Read the notice with care. Check the approved years and tax steps, or ask for an explanation or an official review.

blocks.text: The CRA prefers its online DTC form. For paper, use the latest T2201. From September 8, 2026, versions from before 2023 are no longer accepted.

items.title: “A non-refundable credit is useless if the approved person owes no tax.”
items.text: A family member who supports you may sometimes claim the part you cannot use, and approval can matter for other programs. Each claim and program has its own rules.

blocks.text: From July 14, 2026, do not use the CRA’s general Submit Documents service for a new DTC application unless the CRA asks you for more information.
The DTC depends on severe, long-lasting effects on daily life, not a diagnosis alone.
blocks.detail: Build clear, honest evidence, let your practitioner certify within their role and let the CRA decide.

sections.title: Leah and the Form That Did Not Know Tuesday

paragraphs: Leah Cardinal lived in Winnipeg and managed a long-term condition that made everyday tasks hard to predict. She wanted the Disability Tax Credit approved before tax season, because therapy and medication costs took a big bite out of every month.

She had a well-documented diagnosis, so she expected the form to be easy. Her first draft named the condition three times and said almost nothing about her days. A friend who had been turned down warned her. The diagnosis knew who it was. The form did not know Tuesday.

Leah pushed back, then reread her draft. She had described her hardest day as if it happened every day, and she had left out the supports that made other days possible: a timer on her phone, a rail on the stairs and an hour of rest after lunch.

Her appointment with her nurse practitioner was two days away. She could hand over the folder and ask for it to be made to work, or spend two weeks writing down what her days looked like. The deadline pushed her toward the first choice. She chose the second. Each night she logged which tasks were hard, how long they took and what help she used, on better days and harder days, without exaggerating.

At the appointment, the log changed the conversation. Her hard days were not rare. They were most days, and some tasks took far longer than she had noticed. Her practitioner asked about a second activity she had never mentioned. Leah brought questions, not a prewritten conclusion, and the practitioner certified using clinical judgment.

She sent the online application and kept every copy, including the reference number. The CRA made the decision. The first line of her log, a plain note about a Tuesday in March, stayed pinned above her desk. The application now told one consistent, truthful story.

blocks.text: A short diary can show a pattern that memory squeezes flat. Note your usual days, the help you use and how long things take. Do not exaggerate, play things down or steer a practitioner toward an answer you have already picked.
Leah's diagnosis was never the problem. Her first draft just didn't show a Tuesday.
blocks.detail: Two weeks of simple notes turned a vague form into a clear picture her practitioner could certify with confidence.
blocks.extra: Then a quick check, and a short file to bring to your appointment.

sections.title: Quick Check: Choose the Best Next Move

items.title: Why is a diagnosis alone not enough for the DTC?
items.detail: The CRA decides based on severe, long-lasting effects on daily life under the legal rules, not the name of the diagnosis.

items.title: What five lenses belong in a record of daily impact?
items.detail: Function, frequency, time, support and duration.

items.title: What does “all or almost all of the time” usually mean?
items.detail: Usually at least 90% of the time.

items.title: Who certifies the effects, and who decides eligibility?
items.detail: A health practitioner certifies the condition and its effects. The CRA decides who qualifies.

items.title: Which form version and sending rules apply in 2026?
items.detail: Use the online form or the latest T2201. From September 8, 2026, versions from before 2023 are not accepted. From July 14, do not use the general Submit Documents service for a new application unless the CRA asks.

sections.title: Your Action (Fill Out Form): Your Daily Impact Evidence File

blocks.text: Short answers in plain words. Please do not enter your health card number, SIN, medical records or practitioner login details here. This is preparation, not tax or medical advice.
Keep copies of your application, reference number, practitioner’s form and CRA notice. A tidy file cannot decide who qualifies, but it can head off paperwork mix-ups you could avoid.

items.title: DTC
items.text: Disability Tax Credit. A credit that can lower your income tax.

items.title: Marked restriction
items.text: You cannot do a task, or it takes about three times as long as it would for others your age.

items.title: Prolonged
items.text: Lasting, or expected to last, at least 12 months in a row.

items.title: Cumulative effect
items.text: Several serious limits that together meet the test, even if none meets it alone.

items.title: Life-sustaining therapy
items.text: Therapy you need to keep a vital body function going, under set rules.

items.title: T2201
items.text: The Disability Tax Credit Certificate form.

items.title: Supporting family member
items.text: A person who may claim your unused amount when the transfer rules are met.

quiz.question: True or False: “Only visible or physical disabilities can qualify.”

questions: Which everyday task is hardest for you, or for the person you are helping, and how long has it been going on?
On an ordinary day, how does it show up, and how often? (Every day or almost every day / A few times a week / Now and then / Not sure)
What help, treatment or tools do you already use? Write “none” if there are none.
What is one thing you will do before you apply or call the CRA?
samples: Getting dressed in the morning. About three years.
Almost every day. Buttons and socks take me close to half an hour.
A dressing aid, pain medicine and help from my partner.
Keep a two-week diary to bring to my appointment.
